slides.title: A mapping must answer where and whether
keyPoints: Location and access rights travel together
An entry can lead to another table or to a frame
The requested operation affects the answer
slides.narration: A table that returns a frame number but ignores access rights is not a complete protection model. Reading, writing, and fetching an instruction can require different permissions. A page-table entry therefore carries control information as well as location information. At one level it may point to another table; at a leaf it may describe the mapped page. The exact encoding belongs to the architecture and configuration, not to a guessed C++ struct layout. Our added programs use explicit small fields to explain decomposition and combined checks. They neither read nor modify the operating system’s active page tables.

question.prompt: Why can a known frame number still be insufficient to permit a write?

slides.title: Split a tiny address into two indexes and an offset
keyPoints: Model width: eight bits
Two bits per table index; four offset bits
Reconstruction checks that no address bits disappeared
slides.narration: The address one hundred seven is hexadecimal six B. In this eight-bit model, four low bits give offset eleven, the next two give leaf index two, and the top two give root index one. The program prints those fields and reconstructs one hundred seven from them. This verifies decomposition only; it does not prove that root entry one or leaf entry two is present. A page-table walk would use those indexes to inspect entries and permissions. The small geometry keeps every operation visible. Actual x86-64 examples use different index widths and canonical-address rules, so copying these shifts into system code would be incorrect.

slides.title: A missing entry can have several meanings
keyPoints: Absent hardware translation does not identify the policy
Demand-zero, file-backed, and invalid regions differ
The kernel consults additional mapping information
slides.narration: An absent entry stops the current hardware translation path, but it does not say what recovery is allowed. A valid anonymous region may need a zero-filled page. A valid file mapping may need file data that is already cached or must be read. An address outside every permitted region should be rejected. Treating every absence as permission to allocate would turn invalid accesses into silently accepted memory. The chapter separates the present indicator from the kernel’s policy metadata for this reason. When debugging a fault, identify the mapping policy and requested operation before assuming the device or disk is involved.

question.prompt: Does present=false necessarily mean the page must be read from disk?
question.answer: No. It may need zero-filled backing, already cached data, or rejection as an invalid access.

slides.title: A permissive leaf cannot cancel a restrictive parent
keyPoints: This model combines write permission with logical AND
Leaf-only checking returns the wrong answer
Every required present and user bit also participates
slides.narration: The root entry is present and user-accessible but not writable. The leaf is present, user-accessible, and writable. A careless leaf-only check prints true for a user write. The complete simplified check prints false because the path includes a nonwritable root. For a read, the same present and user conditions pass, so the model prints true. These results follow the explicit AND rule defined here; this struct is not an actual x86 page-table encoding. The lesson is to identify every level whose permissions constrain access rather than choosing the most convenient bit. The requested operation must be part of that decision.

keyPoints: The entry groups flags that describe one mapping. Presence and permission answer different questions, so neither can replace the other. A plausible alternative: A flat table is easy to model; real multilevel tables reduce storage for sparse address spaces at the cost of more involved walks.

slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: A page-table entry encodes mapping information and control bits.
Depending on its level and configuration, it can point to another table or describe a mapped page.
It may include a physical address, presence information, access permissions, and status used by memory-management policy.
An entry is not a portable C structure whose bit layout can be guessed from a diagram for another architecture.
slides.narration:
A page-table entry encodes mapping information and control bits. Depending on its level and configuration, it can point to another table or describe a mapped page. It may include a physical address, presence information, access permissions, and status used by memory-management policy. An entry is not a portable C structure whose bit layout can be guessed from a diagram for another architecture. Kernel code must follow the architecture’s encoding and required update procedures. Ordinary user programs should reason about the behavior exposed by mapping APIs instead of attempting to manipulate active page tables.

In plain English: The program uses a map of memory addresses. The operating system translates that map to where the data is actually stored.

keyPoints: A present indicator tells hardware whether an entry is valid for the corresponding translation step.
An absent entry can cause a page fault.
The kernel may use nonpresent encodings and its own metadata to remember whether the region is demand-paged, swapped, invalid, or associated with another policy.
Therefore, “not present” does not automatically mean “read this page from disk.” The handler must first establish that the access is legitimate.

slides.title: Multilevel page tables
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: A multilevel design divides the virtual page number into several indexes.
Each index selects an entry in the current table; that entry leads to the next level until a mapping is found.
Large-page entries can terminate a walk earlier when the architecture supports them.
A familiar x86-64 example uses four levels with 9 index bits per level and a 12-bit offset, describing a 48-bit virtual-address organization subject to canonical-address rules.

slides.title: Page-table walks
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: A page-table walk follows the hierarchy to resolve a translation.
Hardware performs walks on the reference architecture, potentially using internal caches for table information.
The naive count of one ordinary memory access per level is a useful upper-level teaching model but not a complete performance prediction.
A walk can stop because it finds a valid leaf mapping, encounters an absent entry, or detects a protection problem.
slides.narration:
A page-table walk follows the hierarchy to resolve a translation. Hardware performs walks on the reference architecture, potentially using internal caches for table information. The naive count of one ordinary memory access per level is a useful upper-level teaching model but not a complete performance prediction. A walk can stop because it finds a valid leaf mapping, encounters an absent entry, or detects a protection problem. Once a translation is cached in a TLB, later accesses can avoid repeating the full walk until the entry is evicted or invalidated. The next chapter separates translation caching from data caching.

In plain English: The program uses a map of memory addresses. The operating system translates that map to where the data is actually stored.

The naive count of one ordinary memory access per level is a useful upper-level teaching model but not a complete performance prediction. A walk can stop because it finds a valid leaf mapping, encounters an absent entry, or detects a protection problem. Once a translation is cached in a TLB, later accesses can avoid repeating the full walk until the entry is evicted or invalidated. The next chapter separates translation caching from data caching.

slides.title: A two-level address decomposition
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: Use a 16-bit teaching address space with 256-byte pages and two levels of 16-entry tables.
The address fields are:
Address 0xABCD yields outer index 0xA , inner index 0xB , and offset 0xCD .
Suppose outer entry A points to a valid inner table and inner entry B maps frame 0x34 .
slides.narration:
Use a 16-bit teaching address space with 256-byte pages and two levels of 16-entry tables. The address fields are: Address 0xABCD yields outer index 0xA , inner index 0xB , and offset 0xCD . Suppose outer entry A points to a valid inner table and inner entry B maps frame 0x34 . The translated address is 0x34CD in a physical model that supports that frame number. Now add permissions. The outer entry allows user reads and writes, but the inner entry allows only user reads. A user load succeeds; a user store fails. For this model, effective permissions are the intersection of the permissions along the path. Giving the outer entry more authority cannot override a restrictive leaf entry. A flat table for all 256 virtual pages needs 256 entries. The two-level arrangement needs one 16-entry outer table plus 16 entries for each allocated inner table. With only one populated inner table, it uses 32 entries; with all 16 inner tables allocated, it uses 272 entries. Hierarchy saves space for sparse mappings but is not automatically smaller for a fully populated tiny address space.

In plain English: Think of an address written on a note: the note can tell you where to look, but it does not prove the thing is still there or that you are allowed to use it.

slides.title: Sparse mappings motivate multiple table levels
keyPoints: A flat table reserves entries for the full modeled space
A hierarchy can omit unused subtrees
More levels introduce walking and metadata costs
slides.narration: Imagine a large virtual space where a process uses only a few separated regions. A flat table would reserve a slot for every virtual page even across unused gaps. A hierarchy groups pages under intermediate entries, allowing an unused group to have no allocated lower-level table. This trades some lookup structure for reduced metadata in sparse cases. The tradeoff is not a promise that all page-table walks cost one fixed number of memory loads. Hardware can cache intermediate information and support large-page leaves that end a walk early. Explain both why the hierarchy exists and which caches may hide some of its cost.
actions: Require a concrete mapping, access, or state example before revealing the answer.

question.prompt: Why can multilevel tables save metadata for a sparse address space?
question.answer: Unused address ranges can omit entire lower-level table subtrees instead of allocating one flat entry per possible page.

slides.title: User permission and application authorization are different
keyPoints: User mode may access a buffer
A particular client may still lack permission to see its contents
Memory protection does not know application roles
slides.narration: Suppose a server stores two clients’ records in the same user-accessible heap. Hardware allows the server’s thread to read those bytes. That permission does not authorize sending one client’s record to another client. Page-table user permissions separate execution privilege domains; the application still enforces account and data-access policy. Conversely, a correct account check cannot make a supervisor-only mapping readable from user mode. These are different boundaries with different evidence. In a review, name the subject of each permission: processor privilege, process credentials, or authenticated application identity. Calling all three access control without distinction makes debugging and security reasoning imprecise.
actions: Require a concrete mapping, access, or state example before revealing the answer.

question.prompt: Does a user-accessible page mean every logged-in user should be able to receive its data?
question.answer: No. Hardware access by the process and application-level disclosure authorization are separate decisions.

slides.title: Execute permission applies to instruction fetch
keyPoints: Reading data and fetching instructions are different accesses
Writable data need not be executable
Permission policy must cover each operation
slides.narration: A page can hold bytes that are readable as data without being permitted as instructions. This distinction supports separating writable storage from executable code. Do not model every operation with one Boolean called allowed and then assume the same result applies to reads, writes, and execution. Instead identify the requested access and combine the relevant permissions. Our short lab intentionally models only reads and writes, so it does not prove an execution policy. If instruction fetch is added, give it an explicit access kind and tests. This makes the omission visible and prevents a future feature from silently inheriting the wrong permission meaning.
actions: Require a concrete mapping, access, or state example before revealing the answer.

question.prompt: Does the source read/write model establish whether a page is executable?
question.answer: No. Execution permission is outside that model until an explicit access kind and rule are added.

slides.title: Changing the table does not erase cached translations
keyPoints: A processor may retain an old mapping or permission
Invalidation must reach relevant execution contexts
Multicore coordination is part of the update contract
slides.narration: Suppose the kernel changes a mapping from writable to read-only. If a processor still uses a cached translation with the older writable permission, merely updating memory does not complete the intended revocation. The architecture supplies invalidation mechanisms, and the kernel coordinates them with relevant processors and mapping changes. This is why table updates require a protocol, not just a store to a struct field. Our models omit actual translation caches unless explicitly introduced. When interpreting their output, remember that a successful model lookup cannot verify real invalidation ordering. The next chapter adds cached translation state so this dependency becomes visible.
actions: Require a concrete mapping, access, or state example before revealing the answer.

question.prompt: Why might another core need notification after a mapping change?
question.answer: It may retain a relevant cached translation or permission based on the old table state.

The pure allows function is easy to test and has no state changes. Architecture-specific user/supervisor and execute permissions are outside this limited model and would need explicit fields and checks.

slides.title: Test denied cases as complete paths
keyPoints: Present=false overrides permissive-looking fields
Read-only must reject writes
User access must respect every required level
slides.narration: A useful protection test suite should not stop after one successful read. Try an absent entry whose other flags are true, a present read-only entry with a write request, and a user request through a supervisor-only path. In the two-level model, vary the parent and leaf separately. These cases expose an implementation that accidentally reads only one field or one level. The compiler can verify enum types and function signatures, but it cannot infer the intended permission algebra. State that algebra beside the tests so a maintenance change cannot replace AND with OR while still looking syntactically reasonable.

slides.title: Describe a walk as a sequence of justified steps
keyPoints: Decode indexes under a stated geometry
Check each encountered entry
Finish with a permitted mapping or a defined failure
slides.narration: To explain a page-table walk, begin with the address model rather than a memorized number of levels. Extract the next index, inspect that entry, and determine whether it is present, a pointer to another level, or an allowed leaf. Carry applicable permission restrictions forward. At the end, combine the selected frame with the original offset only if the requested operation is permitted. An absent or restrictive step changes the result. This reasoning transfers from our two-level exercise to more complex architectures without pretending their encodings match. A strong explanation identifies what was checked, not merely that the walk eventually found a number.
